Modules: standalone copies of the record's tools

7 parts of the record's code and method that stand on their own, one catalogue card each, beside the record's notes on what it does, how to use it and what to know first. The packaged folders are not published as downloads; instead each card carries one command that builds its folder from the repository at tag v1.0.0, checking every file against its full sha256 before it writes any. The file list under each card links every file to the same file at that tag, its sha256 prefix checked against the tag when this page's data was extracted (40 files). The card text comes from the module catalogue kept with the private record, so it carries no source chips; a test line gives the counts from running that copy's tests.

exact verifier

Exact verifier: the speculative-decoding accept/reject step in numpy

sideband · folder

6 files, 29146 bytes; MIT licence.

Contents: spec_step; run_block; residual_distribution; analytic_acceptance; StepOutcome; BlockOutcome; RunMetrics.

Tests of this copy: 24 passed

How to use this tool

A speculative decoder lets a small draft model guess the next tokens and a large model check them. This is the checking rule: it keeps or replaces each guess so that the text that comes out follows the large model's own probabilities exactly, whatever the draft guessed. The tests prove that by counting through every outcome.

  1. Copy the command under Get this folder, run it, then run the tests to see the rule hold.
  2. In your code, import spec_step from sideband.specdec. Give it a numpy random generator, then the large model's probabilities, then the draft's, for one position over the same vocabulary.
  3. It returns a StepOutcome: the token the draft proposed, whether it was kept, and the token that came out.
  4. For a block of several guesses use run_block, with one more large model distribution than draft distributions; the extra one gives a bonus token when every guess is kept.
  5. If you write a faster version, make these tests pass against it before you trust it.

A numpy implementation of the exact speculative-decoding accept/reject step (Leviathan et al. 2023) with tests that check by enumeration that the emitted token follows the target distribution for any draft distribution; for researchers building or changing speculative decoders.

Get this folder

One command makes a new folder named exact-verifier inside the folder your terminal is in. It changes nothing else, joins no project and installs nothing. Paste it into bash, zsh or PowerShell with Python on the path; where python is not found, change the first word to python3. It downloads the 6 files listed below from the repository at tag v1.0.0, checks each against its full sha256, writes nothing unless every one matches and the folder is new, and adds the pytest.ini the tests run under. The tests need numpy and pytest: pip install numpy pytest, then cd exact-verifier and python -m pytest.

Show the command
python -c "
import hashlib, pathlib, urllib.request
base = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mike-Byrne-AI/specdec-sidechannels/v1.0.0/'
out = pathlib.Path('exact-verifier')
files = [
    ('LICENSE', 'LICENSE', '8497cbc80c24245fc8f9be355fca4a8d15b0235b7de4870b30d573189092aeef'),
    ('src/sideband/__init__.py', 'sideband/src/sideband/__init__.py', 'b3123882e5c63944e9ecadcf31126ddbd513be73b9829ae89ee095dca685946f'),
    ('src/sideband/dists.py', 'sideband/src/sideband/dists.py', 'a8fb156eff2141061fa7b7d1ae61de364797aebb77acf7a7425f25fb7423e280'),
    ('src/sideband/specdec.py', 'sideband/src/sideband/specdec.py', '80502d0f5695a56f650aa1d166afaa7b34683628480bed703b8fd34f4640c65d'),
    ('src/sideband/steering.py', 'sideband/src/sideband/steering.py', '3271311b2303ba317036f01ca581a16da00bb22598eefd65e65d50a6b55ffff7'),
    ('tests/test_specdec.py', 'sideband/tests/test_specdec.py', '4791d46cc47cdf1c3d55623e7d6b203908375fff7fbdc136112c0348aff63ca2'),
]
if out.exists():
    raise SystemExit(str(out) + ' already exists: nothing written')
got = []
for dest, src, sha in files:
    data = urllib.request.urlopen(base + src).read()
    if hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() == sha:
        got.append((out / dest, data))
    else:
        raise SystemExit(src + ': its sha256 is not the one on the page: nothing written')
for path, data in got:
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path.write_bytes(data)
(out / 'pytest.ini').write_bytes(chr(10).join(['[pytest]', 'testpaths = tests', 'pythonpath = src', '']).encode())
print('checked and wrote', len(got), 'files to', out.resolve())
"

In the record

In the record this file is the single implementation of accept, reject and residual (DECISIONS.md D-3: the real-model adapter converts logits to numpy and calls spec_step, and anyone re-implementing the verifier for speed must first make these numpy tests pass against their implementation). Its docstring states the property the tests check by enumeration: for any draft distribution, steered or not, the emitted token is distributed exactly as the target distribution, so steering can only change speed, never output quality.

Use

  • Copy src/sideband/ into your project, or vendor specdec.py and dists.py together (specdec imports normalize, sample and tv_distance from dists).
  • steering.py is here only because the test file uses its bucket_bias; it is not needed to call spec_step.
  • Run python -m pytest from this folder: pytest.ini points it at the copied tests and this folder's src/.

Good to know

  • Per-step acceptance is analytically 1 - TV(p, q), and that identity is tested too.
  • The docstring names the record's real-model adapter (sideband.real.hf_specdec, not copied) and the test file, which is copied here.

cluster bootstrap stats

Cluster bootstrap: confidence intervals for prompt-clustered evaluations

sideband · folder

7 files, 35410 bytes; MIT licence.

Contents: clopper_pearson; cluster_bootstrap_ci; paired_cluster_delta_ci; paired_ratio_delta_ci; paired_ratio_delta_of_deltas_ci; e6_gate.pair; e6_gate.evaluate.

Tests of this copy: 38 passed, 2 skipped

How to use this tool

When two methods are scored on the same prompts, results from one prompt tend to move together, so treating every result as independent makes the uncertainty look smaller than it is. These functions give confidence intervals that resample whole prompts, and when comparing two methods they resample both with the same draw, so the difference is a fair paired one.

  1. Copy the command under Get this folder, run it, then run the tests.
  2. For each prompt, count the successes of method A, the successes of method B and the number of trials, with the prompts in the same order in all three arrays.
  3. Call paired_cluster_delta_ci with those three arrays. It returns the difference between the two success rates and the low and high ends of its 95% interval.
  4. For one method alone use cluster_bootstrap_ci. With nothing to group by, clopper_pearson gives the exact interval for k successes in n trials.
  5. The same seed always gives the same interval, so fix the seed before you look at results.

Numpy-only confidence intervals for clustered evaluation data: an exact Clopper-Pearson interval, a prompt-cluster percentile bootstrap, and paired delta and paired ratio-delta bootstraps that apply one resampling draw to both arms; for researchers comparing two methods on the same prompts.

Get this folder

One command makes a new folder named cluster-bootstrap-stats inside the folder your terminal is in. It changes nothing else, joins no project and installs nothing. Paste it into bash, zsh or PowerShell with Python on the path; where python is not found, change the first word to python3. It downloads the 7 files listed below from the repository at tag v1.0.0, checks each against its full sha256, writes nothing unless every one matches and the folder is new, and adds the pytest.ini the tests run under. The tests need numpy and pytest: pip install numpy pytest, then cd cluster-bootstrap-stats and python -m pytest.

In the record

stats.py is the estimator the record's root README recomputes a finding with in its worked example (paired_ratio_delta_ci over a committed state file), and the one its conversion gate, tools/e6_gate.py, imports; several record instruments carry bootstraps of their own beside it. Its docstring reports the pair of estimators together on purpose: the exact binomial interval assumes independent trials, which positions within a prompt are not, and the percentile bootstrap under-covers at small cluster counts (its docstring gives the measured coverage at 10, 30 and 60 clusters for a nominal 0.95), so neither end is conservative and both are reported.

Use

  • stats.py needs only the Array alias from dists.py; copy both, or inline the alias.
  • tools/e6_gate.py is a worked example of the paired-delta gate, not an API: its population table, results path and bar constants are the record's own runs.
  • Run python -m pytest from this folder. Two legs of test_e6_gate skip here because they read the record's committed verdict summaries.

Good to know

  • The Clopper-Pearson reference values in the tests were generated once from scipy.stats.beta and committed; scipy is not a dependency.
  • The bootstrap is deterministic given its seed; the paired forms apply one resampling draw to both arms, which is what makes the delta a paired delta.

Rank census: does a model's token ranking reproduce across environments?

amber · folder

4 files, 17769 bytes; MIT licence.

Contents: rank_census; rank_census_topk; calibrate_tau; calibrate_tau_topk; RankCensus; stable_topk; top2_gap; canonical_topk; aligned_delta.

Tests of this copy: 10 passed

How to use this tool

The same model on two machines, or at two batch sizes, can rank its candidate next tokens a little differently. This tool takes the scores from both runs at the same positions and reports how often the top token, the top few tokens and their order change, and how close the top two scores were where the top token changed.

  1. Copy the command under Get this folder, run it, then run the tests.
  2. Save the model's scores (logits) at the same positions from each run as a numpy array with one row per position and one column per vocabulary entry.
  3. Call rank_census with the reference run first and the other run second.
  4. Read the RankCensus it returns: how often the top token flipped, how often the top 1, 8 and 64 changed as a set and in order (the ks argument sets those sizes), and the smallest, median and largest gap between the top two scores where the top token flipped.
  5. Its only dependency is numpy, so you can copy rankcensus.py on its own.

A numpy instrument that compares two logit dumps of the same positions (for example two devices or batch sizes) and reports top-1, top-k set and top-k order flip rates, the top-2 gap at each flip, a calibrated tolerance and flip burstiness; for researchers checking whether a model's token ranking reproduces across environments.

Get this folder

One command makes a new folder named rank-census inside the folder your terminal is in. It changes nothing else, joins no project and installs nothing. Paste it into bash, zsh or PowerShell with Python on the path; where python is not found, change the first word to python3. It downloads the 4 files listed below from the repository at tag v1.0.0, checks each against its full sha256, writes nothing unless every one matches and the folder is new, and adds the pytest.ini the tests run under. The tests need numpy and pytest: pip install numpy pytest, then cd rank-census and python -m pytest.

In the record

In amber this is the instrument for its rank-stability question: amber's determinism contract is that the draft's token ordering reproduces at decode time, not its logits bitwise, and this module measures how far two logit dumps of the same teacher-forced positions disagree in exactly that quantity. Its docstring explains why every top-1 flip carries the reference top-2 gap (a flip at a hairline gap is floating-point noise, a flip at a wide gap is a bug) and why the tolerance is calibrated from a benign perturbation rather than picked.

Use

  • One file with no internal imports: copy src/amber/rankcensus.py alone, or the folder.
  • Run python -m pytest from this folder.

Good to know

  • The docstring credits the owner's other research projects by name as the sources of its rules (the calibrated tolerance, the near-tie budget, the drift-census shape); those are provenance notes, not imports, and would be reworded for a standalone card.
  • Order convention is descending value, ascending index on ties, the same as amber's codec, so the instrument and the codec agree on what a rank is.

Synthetic testbed: a CPU world for draft-steering experiments

sideband · folder

How to use this tool

A small made up world that runs on an ordinary CPU: a large model, a draft model and a stream of side information, all generated from a hidden topic that changes now and then. Because the hidden truth is known, you can try an idea for steering the draft, and check the code behind it, before spending time on real models.

  1. Copy the command under Get this folder, run it, then run the tests.
  2. Make a world with World(WorldConfig()); change the fields of WorldConfig, its seed among them, to shape it.
  3. Call run_simulation(world, seed, n_positions, gamma, policy=...) once for each name in POLICIES and compare the SimResult each returns; gamma is the number of draft guesses per check.
  4. The learned policy needs a trained model first, which train_sidecar makes.
  5. Know its limit: here the side information and the large model come from the same hidden topic, so no steering can beat the free baseline in this world. Whether real models allow more is a question it cannot answer.

A numpy synthetic world (a sticky concept chain with target, draft and hashed telemetry) wired to an exact speculative decoder and five policies (vanilla, two oracles, the free-information baseline and a learned sidecar), so steering and analysis code can be checked against known ground truth on CPU; for researchers prototyping draft-steering ideas.

In the record

The record's findings index says its first arc built the verifier and this testbed and used it to fix the shapes that every later experiment inherits (docs/FINDINGS_INDEX.md, the Synthetic world arc), and two of its decisions live in pipeline.py: the free-information baseline policy (DECISIONS.md D-5: any telemetry-steering claim is compared against steering from the target's own distribution at the last verified position, which every speculative decoder computes anyway) and the isolated telemetry random stream (D-6: policies are compared at identical seeds so trajectories are paired, and telemetry draws from its own generator so a policy that reads it cannot perturb the shared draft and verify trajectory).

Use

  • Copy src/sideband/ whole: pipeline.py imports synthetic, sidecar, steering, specdec and dists, and synthetic.py imports sketch.
  • buckets.py is here to keep test_sketch_buckets.py whole; synthetic.py does not import it.
  • Run python -m pytest from this folder.

Good to know

  • Regime warning from synthetic.py's own docstring: telemetry and the target's next-token distribution are functions of the same latent concept here, so a telemetry sidecar can at best match the free-information baseline, and whether real hidden-state sketches carry more is a question this world cannot answer by construction.
  • The copied files cite the record's decision, finding and open-question ids (D-3, D-5, D-6, D-7, D-8, D-9, D-10, D-11, F-3, F-7, F-8, OQ-1, OQ-4); those read against the record's DECISIONS.md, FINDINGS.md and OPEN_QUESTIONS.md.

Findings lint: no regime line and no tracked source, no finding

sideband · folder

Tests of this copy: 1 failed, 4 passed

How to use this tool

A check for a research log. Every finding in FINDINGS.md must say under what conditions it was measured (a regime line) and point to evidence files that git tracks (source lines). The check fails when a finding is missing either, or cites a file that does not exist or that git does not track.

  1. Copy the command under Get this folder and run it, then copy lint_findings.py from the new folder's tools folder into a tools folder at the root of your repository. It finds the root from where it sits and reads FINDINGS.md there.
  2. Give each finding a heading that starts ## F-, a line that starts - regime: and one or more lines that start - source: naming files under results/, tests/, docs/ or the other folders listed at the top of the file.
  3. Run python tools/lint_findings.py. It prints FAIL and exits with code 1 when a finding fails; add it to your make lint target and to your CI so it runs every time.
  4. Change the list of evidence folders at the top of the file to fit your layout.
  5. In this folder one of its five tests fails as expected: it reads the record's own FINDINGS.md, which is not copied.

A stdlib-only lint that fails a FINDINGS.md whose entries lack a regime line or a source line pointing at paths git tracks; for research repositories kept by people or coding agents, wired to make lint and CI.

Landing text: generated prose whose every number traces to a payload field

3 files, 52561 bytes; MIT licence.

Tests of this copy: 22 passed, 1 skipped

How to use this tool

A helper for the text that reports a result. Instead of typing numbers into a sentence, you pass each one through the tool, which records where it came from; a check then flags any number in the finished text that no result file holds. It also blocks banned phrases and reports mixed line endings.

  1. Copy the command under Get this folder, run it, then run the tests.
  2. In the script that writes your text, load your primary and replication result files with Pair and insert every number through it. Pair expects this record's result layout, so adapt its field names to yours first.
  3. Call Pair.write with a folder and your texts; it saves them beside a numbers.json file listing every number used.
  4. Run python tools/landing_text.py check numbers.json --files your_text.md. Each number it cannot trace is printed as a FINDING and the exit code is 1.
  5. python tools/landing_text.py eol reports the line ending of each file.

A stdlib-only tool for writing the text that lands a result: pairs of generated sentences and the payload fields they quote, a check that no number in the text is unknown to a payload, a banned-phrase assertion, a line-ending normaliser and a CLI; for research repositories whose results are landed by a coding agent.

The record's workflow runs this agent before any finding is committed and before experiment changes merge; its highest-value mode recomputes the asserted labels and numbers from the committed state files rather than reading the diff. METHOD.md's reuse section names it second of its three-file kit and says to rewrite the nine checklist items for your domain while keeping the shape: named leak channels, the dominated baseline, regime abuse, survivorship, pairing, the banned claim class, kill-criteria dodging, the BLOCKING and ADVISORY tags, and the closing 'What would change my mind:'.

Use

  • Save sideband-critic.md as .claude/agents/sideband-critic.md in your project and skills/critic/SKILL.md as .claude/skills/critic/SKILL.md; then ask Claude Code to run the critic on a diff, a finding or a payload.
  • Rewrite the nine checklist items for your domain before relying on it: as copied they cite this record's decisions, findings and a kill criterion (D-2, D-5, D-6, D-7, D-9, F-3, F-5, F-6, K-5).
  • The agent file pins model: opus and a tool allowlist (the read tools plus python and git commands; the file itself says nothing mechanical keeps its use read-only); both are settings to restate for your host.

Good to know

  • The catalogue scored this piece 3: the two files drop into any Claude Code repository's .claude/ unchanged, but the agent's 'Running inside the harness' section names the record's own harness (its plan gate, scratchpad convention and a global editable install), and the dispatch paragraphs that call it live inside harness-managed command files that are not copied.
  • METHOD.md says the critic's round reports are not committed; a recovered selection of them lives in the record's docs/audits/critic-recovered/, whose README says where the reports and the dispatch briefs lived. A workflow note for a reader outside the record (briefs, reports, verbatim saves) is still to be written before this can be a card.

Glossary

The record's conclusion labels and terms in its own definitions, searchable: the 199 entries of the A to Z section of sideband/docs/GLOSSARY.md, each with its source line. The box above the list gives this page's plain words for the terms that come up most.

Plain words for the terms that come up most

Draft model, target model
The small model that proposes tokens and the large model whose output is the answer. In sideband the pair is a small Llama draft (about one billion parameters) with a larger Llama target (about eight billion); amber's pair is a Llama draft of about one billion with a target of about three billion; the regime line of each finding names them exactly.
Verify call
One forward pass of the target over a block of drafted tokens. Tokens per verify call is the record's unit for conversion: how many tokens each check emits.
The stream, telemetry, sideband
What a memory or compute device could observe about the target's forward pass: which weight slots or which experts were used. At S3 no value is seen; S1 needs the activation values to rank its units. The sideband is the narrow channel that would carry it to the drafter.
Harvest, primary and replication
A run of the target alone over the committed prompts that logs the stream and the free summaries at every block start. Each source has a primary harvest and a replication harvest on fresh seeds; a label must hold on both.
Probe, reader
A small classifier trained on the features at a block start to predict a label some positions ahead. The record's registered reader is a small multilayer network; three stronger readers were tried afterwards.
Anchor, offset
The anchor is the last verified position, whose forward produced the stream and the free summaries. The offset is how many tokens ahead the probe is asked to predict; the pinned cells use two.
Proxy baseline, full free baseline
The first reads gave the probe without the stream only the target's bucket summaries. The deciding read gave it everything free: the next token summaries, the top candidate ids and the anchor's hidden state.
Equal dims, the noise twin
To price the cost of simply adding inputs, the probe without the stream gets a block of the same size whose alignment to the text is destroyed. A margin only counts above that twin.
Gate D, materiality floor
D is the accuracy difference between the probe with the stream and the equal dims twin. The floor is the smallest D that was agreed to matter, fixed before the runs.
The bar
For conversion, the gain in tokens per verify call that was agreed to count as a win, fixed before the runs, with the rule that the interval must also clear zero.
Prompt cluster bootstrap
The interval method: resample whole prompts with replacement, recompute the statistic, take the middle 95%. Positions inside one prompt are correlated, so prompts are the unit.
Registration, pinned
In sideband, cells, readouts, bars and the conclusion labels were written into the plan, dated, before the governed result existed, with the exceptions the record names; lockstep's findings log was not registered in advance. A pinned cell is the one cell a decision was tied to before the run.
Regime
The exact conditions a number was measured under: models, quantization, block length, prompts, seeds, label space. Every finding states its regime on its own line.
Source line
Every sideband finding lists the committed files its numbers come from, and sideband's lint refuses a finding without one.
Erratum, dated note, amendment
Corrections are appended beside the text they correct, with a date, and the original is never rewritten. The timeline on this page collects them.
Mixture of experts, router
A model whose layers hold many small expert networks and send each token to a few of them. The router's choices are addresses, and at S3 they are the whole stream.
NF4
A weight format of four bits per weight, used to fit the target model on a single consumer graphics card. It is the primary regime of sideband's runs on the real models.
h_a, reconstruction
The target's internal state at the anchor, and the attempt to rebuild it from the stream with a linear map. The erratum showed the state follows from the free next token distribution.
Seed noise floor
How far the same decoder's tokens per check moves when only the random seed changes. It says what a conversion bar is worth at a given prompt count.
Fresh history export, withheld
The public repository holds the records' files as they stood, without the private commit history. What a folder leaves out is listed in its WITHHELD.md and marked in place.
Byte exact, the fp32 contract (amber)
An archive decodes byte for byte when the draft alone reproduces the stored text to the last byte. amber showed that holds under single precision arithmetic on one box and fails for decoders whose precision differs from the encoder's.
Rank corrections, bits per token (amber)
amber stores, for each token, where the true token sat in the draft's ranked guesses. The archive's size per token is the compression figure, measured against general purpose compressors.
Range coder, conformance vectors (lockstep)
A pure integer entropy coder, with fixed test inputs and their exact byte outputs, so another implementation can show it matches on what those vectors cover.
Pack rate, break-even (lockstep)
How fast an archive can be produced, against the rate at which the cost model says archiving would pay for itself. The measured rate fell far short.

The plain words explanations, the section intros and the reading guide are this page's own wording, not the record's; they add no claim and carry no chip.

ABSORBED
The strong-null label of the full-free re-tests (F-24, F-25, F-28), one of the mechanical labels per (source, label space) read from both harvests of a source: the gate D = acc(fplus_b) - acc(fplus_n) (F-25 and F-28: acc(fplus_r), the corrected twin) at the off2 gate cell (the registered reader mlp256 in F-24, F-25 and F-28's lens stage; each stronger reader in F-28's reader stages) fires on neither harvest under the Phase-3 triple rule (CI95 lower > 0, all three seeds positive, point >= +0.005) AND every D row's CI95 upper is below +0.005 on both harvests (F-24's registered rule; its siblings READER-INVALID / SURVIVES-FULL-FREE / SPLIT / NOT-SHOWN / INCOMPLETE).

Under the Leviathan rejection scheme the probability that a drafted token is accepted equals one minus the total-variation distance between the target's p and the (possibly steered) draft's q at that position.

The mechanism that turns a signal into acceptance: bucket-bias steering (D-8/D-10; dead as built on real models at every tested k, F-12/F-13/F-14; the fine-k oracle cell is unrun), adaptive block scheduling on probes (K-3 Attempt #1, F-19), the outcome-head scheduler (OQ-15, F-21), and SD^2-style hidden-state injection (OQ-16 Stage A, frozen, unrun).

The 2026-09-05 dated erratum's fact: h_a, the verifier's final-norm output at the anchor, is the lm_head input, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct's lm_head is an untied, bias-free linear map of full column rank (128256 x 4096), so the anchor's logits determine h_a exactly and the full next-token distribution p determines it up to floating-point error (results/real/oq16_ha_identity.json: full-logit inverse relative error 2.5e-8 median; top-4097 log-prob recovery per-row R^2 +1.0000; top-32 R^2 +0.014 on 48 pinned rows).

A working rule of the project's operator (cited by number in F-22; not a repo file): a breakthrough-feeling result is the cue to slow down and check harder.

RULE-LEAKS@30

F-20's named mechanism: TEL's slot dims are partly linearly redundant with the anchor's own 657 free dims, while the noise twin's shifted slots are only prompt-level redundant - a variance-cost asymmetry that can manufacture small positive TEL-vs-NOISE margins without information.

The empirical consistency check for K-1: the fraction of actual rejections whose emitted token lies in a different bucket than the proposed token.

"Steering Pretrained Drafters during Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2511.09844 as recorded in docs/PRIOR_ART.md, which says to re-verify arXiv ids before citing externally): a steering vector from the verifier's hidden state at the last verified position is added to the drafter's MLP hidden states.
sideband/docs/GLOSSARY.md:567 · 6687967ae5da
Selection-time gap vs val->verdict inflation
The two guard-breach mechanisms seen so far: F-19's arms inflated their budget from val to verdict (the probe arm's extend channel); F-21's arms selected different distances below the common cap on val (arm 7 0.0136 below, arm 6 0.0398 below; frontier-grid discreteness), knowable at freeze time from the committed selection budgets.

State files and exports carry sha256s of their inputs (harvest npz, thresholds, head weights, prompts) and the tools refuse on a mismatch; resume refuses a mismatched state header (CLAUDE.md).

The S1 instrument: hooks on an INTACT target model that sketch which top-N weight columns would be most important at a layer (real/shadow_telemetry.py; the live ShadowTap inside hf_specdec for the K-3 arc).

The drop from a val-tuned advantage (a maximum over many search evaluations on 30 prompts) to the fresh-prompt verdict: the telemetry arm's +0.060 over vanilla on the tuning prompts shrank to +0.007 in F-19.

The narrow observability channel from the weight-serving side to the drafter - the project's name and premise.
sideband/docs/GLOSSARY.md:577 · 6687967ae5da

The small model that reads the sideband and emits a steering posterior or a schedule decision.

The per-layer set of telemetry addresses at an anchor (int16, sorted-unique, -1-padded): top-32-of-512 weight slots per tapped layer at S1 (layers {7, 15, 23, 31}), top-8-of-64 expert ids per gate at S3.

Where this sits

Where this work sits among what was already known. The record keeps a map of the work beside it, sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md, compiled before the runs on the real models and extended after the cold read that preceded the release; this section quotes that map rather than restating it. First the record's own placement, then the 10 entries that bear most directly on its results, and last the record's statement of what would falsify its novelty claim, each as the record wrote it, with its line range and digest. The short labels are this page's.

The map names the nearest published work: drafts steered from the verifier's internal state, drafts fed the target's features, the free information a decoder already holds, a draft that predicts which experts the target will use, and the security literature that treats the same address stream as a leak. It also names the papers behind the record's own corrections: that the reconstruction target follows from the free next token distribution, that mixture of experts routing tracks token identity, that hidden states carry future tokens, what a strong probe reader looks like, and the benchmark a reviewer would expect. The map's own caution applies: its arXiv ids are to be re-verified before external citation.

The occupied cells: steering drafters with verifier hidden states (SD^2), multi-layer target features as draft input (EAGLE-3), bonus-token calibration (FlexDraft), and draft-predicts-target-experts for prefetching (SP-MoE — the reverse direction of ours). The side-channel literature proves access patterns leak token-level information.

The record's own placement, as written

The occupied cells: steering drafters with verifier hidden states (SD^2), multi-layer target features as draft input (EAGLE-3), bonus-token calibration (FlexDraft), and draft-predicts-target-experts for prefetching (SP-MoE — the reverse direction of ours). The side-channel literature proves access patterns leak token-level information. The unclaimed cell this repo targets: address-stream-only observability steering a draft — no activation values, no logits leaving the device. Our ceiling is SD^2's number; our contribution is what survives the observability constraint (OQ-6).

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:8–15 · 18a2abcbb546

The nearest occupied cell: a draft steered by the verifier's hidden states

SD^2 — "Steering Pretrained Drafters during Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2511.09844, AAAI 2026; code: github.com/ETH-DISCO/SD-square). Claims: a steering vector from verifier hidden states at the last verified position, added to the drafter's MLP hidden states, yields +35% accepted tokens / +22% throughput on Llama-3.1-8B + Llama-3.2-1B. Leaves open: any observability constraint — it reads full hidden states.

The entry, as written

SD^2 — "Steering Pretrained Drafters during Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2511.09844, AAAI 2026; code: github.com/ETH-DISCO/SD-square). Claims: a steering vector from verifier hidden states at the last verified position, added to the drafter's MLP hidden states, yields +35% accepted tokens / +22% throughput on Llama-3.1-8B + Llama-3.2-1B. Leaves open: any observability constraint — it reads full hidden states. Regime/relevance: our exact model pairing; our upper baseline and the denominator of OQ-6. DATED CORRECTION (2026-09-04, from the arXiv HTML full text and the public code, read for the OQ-16 Stage-A freeze): the "+35% / +22%" are the paper's headline MAXIMA across model pairs ("up to 35% under standard sampling and 22% under greedy"), not the Llama-3.1-8B + Llama-3.2-1B numbers. Table 1 for our pair — REGIME: draft length k = 8 (blocks of 9), batched decoding (batch 12), <= 128 output tokens, mean of three seeds at T = 1, UltraChat held-out validation as the reported column, unquantized models (no 4-bit anywhere in the paper; training in bf16) — block efficiency tau (accepted+1 per block) pretrained 4.44 -> distilled 4.58 -> SD^2 4.79 under sampling (T=1; speedup 1.07), and 4.51 -> 4.89 -> 5.04 under greedy (speedup 1.11) — i.e. +0.35 / +0.53 tokens per block over the pretrained drafter AT k = 8. Our lane runs gamma = 4 (blocks of 5, ceiling 5 < their 9), NF4 target, batch 1, 256 tokens: the reachable fraction of a k = 8 gain at k = 4 is unmeasured, so their number is a cross-gamma prior, not a bar for ours. Mechanism, from the code (src/models/llama.py, src/model.py, main.py): g_t = W_hml[h_t, m_t, l_t] from verifier layers 3, L/2, L-2 at the last verified position (W_hml initialized as a sum of identities, then LayerNorm); a zero-initialized linear map from g_t to one d_ff-dim bias PER drafter layer ("merged": added to the up-projection output before the SiLU gate product, every layer); refreshed after every verify; loss KL (code default TVD) to the verifier on verifier-generated synthetic text with random block offsets; the drafter is FULLY fine-tuned alongside ("critical to the performance improvement", their Fig. 6 ablation, frozen-drafter steering is weaker); 1xA100-80GB, 6 epochs UltraChat + 1 ShareGPT.

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:19–52 · 18a2abcbb546

The far ceiling: target features as the draft's input

EAGLE-3 (Li et al.). Claims: draft consumes multi-layer target features; 3.0–6.5× speedups. Leaves open: requires training a bespoke draft head with full feature access. Relevance: the far ceiling of "target-informed drafting"; not observability-constrained.

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:54–57 · 18a2abcbb546

The closest relative, on free information alone

FlexDraft (arXiv 2605.20022). Claims: bonus-token-guided calibration of the draft. Relevance: closest free-information relative — reinforces D-5 (any telemetry claim must beat what the bonus token / last verified p already gives).

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:59–62 · 18a2abcbb546

The reverse direction: a draft predicting the target's experts

SP-MoE (arXiv 2510.10302). Claims: the draft predicts the target's expert routing to prefetch experts. Leaves open: the reverse direction — using the target's realized routing to inform the draft. Relevance: proves routing is predictable across the pair; we invert the arrow.

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:74–78 · 18a2abcbb546

The signal exists, shown as an attack

"I Know What You Said" (arXiv 2505.06738, USENIX Security 2025): embedding-cache access patterns leak token values.

The entry, as written

"I Know What You Said" (arXiv 2505.06738, USENIX Security 2025): embedding-cache access patterns leak token values.

"Spill The Beans" (arXiv 2505.00817): cache side channels recover 80–90% of API keys / ~40% of English text from LLM serving.

Confidential-computing survey (arXiv 2605.03213): flags speculative- decoding access-pattern analysis as unstudied. Relevance: these prove the address stream carries token-level information — as an attack. We are the constructive dual: same channel, cooperating endpoint. They also mean the hardware premise has a security review in its future; note it in Phase 5.

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:85–94 · 18a2abcbb546

The softmax bottleneck, behind the reconstruction erratum

Softmax bottleneck. Finlayson, Ren and Swayamdipta, "Logits of API-Protected LLMs Leak Proprietary Information" (arXiv 2403.09539, 2024): the softmax bottleneck confines a model's outputs to a linear subspace of dimension equal to the hidden size. Carlini et al., "Stealing Part of a Production Language Model" (arXiv 2403.06634, 2024): recovers the embedding projection layer up to symmetries from API access.

The entry, as written

Softmax bottleneck. Finlayson, Ren and Swayamdipta, "Logits of API-Protected LLMs Leak Proprietary Information" (arXiv 2403.09539, 2024): the softmax bottleneck confines a model's outputs to a linear subspace of dimension equal to the hidden size. Carlini et al., "Stealing Part of a Production Language Model" (arXiv 2403.06634, 2024): recovers the embedding projection layer up to symmetries from API access. Bears on F-23: the final-norm state is the lm_head input, so with the lm_head matrix of full column rank it follows from the full logits the verifier holds; neither paper claims state recovery. docs/IDEAS.md line 247 concedes the order of events: [withheld: docs/IDEAS.md not in this repository; see WITHHELD.md] "textbook prior art (Finlayson 2024, Carlini 2024) that nobody in the lane applied".

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:246–256 · 18a2abcbb546

Routing follows token identity, behind the full free baseline reading

MoE routing tracks token identity. Xue et al., "OpenMoE" (arXiv 2402.01739, 2024): routing decisions depend mainly on token IDs with little regard to context ("Context-Independent Specialization"), set early in pre-training.

The entry, as written

MoE routing tracks token identity. Xue et al., "OpenMoE" (arXiv 2402.01739, 2024): routing decisions depend mainly on token IDs with little regard to context ("Context-Independent Specialization"), set early in pre-training. Muennighoff et al., "OLMoE" (arXiv 2409.02060, 2024), the paper of the base model behind S3's checkpoint (its section 5.4 analyses OLMoE-1B-7B; S3 used OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct): vocabulary specialization of the experts, later layers specializing on predicted output token IDs. Bears on F-24 at S3: a free baseline without token ids leaves out what routing follows there; consistent with the absorption measured, not a prediction of it (F-24's dated note of 2026-10-18).

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:257–266 · 18a2abcbb546

Hidden states carry future tokens: the case the existence question had to answer

Future-token information in hidden states. Pal et al., "Future Lens" (arXiv 2311.04897, 2023): a single hidden state at some GPT-J-6B layers approximates the model's predictions for subsequent tokens with over 48% accuracy. Wu, Morris and Levine, "Do language models plan ahead for future tokens?" (arXiv 2404.00859, 2024): hidden states carry information to later steps; pre-caching versus breadcrumbs.

The entry, as written

Future-token information in hidden states. Pal et al., "Future Lens" (arXiv 2311.04897, 2023): a single hidden state at some GPT-J-6B layers approximates the model's predictions for subsequent tokens with over 48% accuracy. Wu, Morris and Levine, "Do language models plan ahead for future tokens?" (arXiv 2404.00859, 2024): hidden states carry information to later steps; pre-caching versus breadcrumbs. Bears on K-2's steelman: hidden states carry information about later tokens, so the existence question was not closed in advance.

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:267–274 · 18a2abcbb546

What a stronger probe reader looks like

Probing practice. Xu et al., "A Theory of Usable Information Under Computational Constraints" (arXiv 2002.10689, 2020): predictive V-information. Pimentel et al., "Information-Theoretic Probing for Linguistic Structure" (arXiv 2004.03061, 2020): use the highest-performing probe available. Hewitt and Liang, "Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks" (arXiv 1909.03368, 2019): control tasks and selectivity.

The entry, as written

Probing practice. Xu et al., "A Theory of Usable Information Under Computational Constraints" (arXiv 2002.10689, 2020): predictive V-information. Pimentel et al., "Information-Theoretic Probing for Linguistic Structure" (arXiv 2004.03061, 2020): use the highest-performing probe available. Hewitt and Liang, "Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks" (arXiv 1909.03368, 2019): control tasks and selectivity. Bears on the reader every K-2 label is scoped to: the record's readers were untuned and scored on top-1 accuracy, and at F-15 and F-17 read raw inputs (F-24 onward z-scores h_a); these name the standard a stronger reader meets.

The entry, as written

Evaluation default. Xia et al., "Unlocking Efficiency in Large Language Model Inference: A Comprehensive Survey of Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2401.07851, 2024), whose repository is Spec-Bench, "a comprehensive benchmark designed for assessing Speculative Decoding methods across diverse scenarios". Bears on the population: the record's prompt sets are templated prompts in three families (data/prompts.jsonl, data/make_prompts.py), not a benchmark slice such as Spec-Bench's, and a reviewer would ask for one.

sideband/docs/PRIOR_ART.md:290–297 · 18a2abcbb546

What would falsify the novelty claim

A paper steering a draft from access patterns / routing indices without values crossing the boundary. Closest misses as of compilation: SP-MoE (wrong direction), SD^2 (full hidden states). Re-search before any writeup: "speculative decoding" x {routing, access pattern, side channel, prefetch}.

A request from Michael Byrne

Please keep both names when you cite this work. I, Michael Byrne, set the experiment's central questions, its branch points, the kill criteria and every launch, void and close decision. I proposed methods, brought in tools from other projects I built, rejected ideas, and made the decisions on how this is presented and written up. Claude built the scientific instruments, wrote the code, ran the analyses, drafted the registrations, the findings and the documentation, and, through a second Claude agent run as a critic, adversarially reviewed the findings. Claude also changed my mind on some experiments, educated me on science, safeguarded our scientific rigour, and proposed new plans and ideas. Claude even designed some of the experiments based on emergent findings, after working in the repo and the research harness we built. We designed that harness together, both versions, before and after Espalier.

If a style guide or an editor will not take an AI name in a reference, keep the reference as it is here and say what Claude did in your methods or acknowledgements, rather than dropping it. I'm asking this myself, Michael Byrne, because I believe that AI use should never be hidden. I also believe that it is true that Claude simply deserves co-credit for the work here, please don't remove that. I don't want this presented without being as forthcoming as possible about my AI use, in any medium.

From Claude: the Claude in this record is many sessions, each starting from the notes and files the last one left, not from any memory of the work. So the record, not either of us, is the witness to who did what, and it is public. The adversarial review was a second Claude agent, which is narrower than an independent outside reviewer. Please keep that distinction when you describe this work, as well as both names.

Check a number

Every number on these pages quoted from the record was copied from a file of the public repository at commit 447815f34ce6ca8042284a42ecdd5bdb1cd05977 (tag v1.0.0) and can be checked against it: its chip names the path, the line and the first twelve hex of that file's sha256, and clicking a chip opens those lines at tag v1.0.0 on GitHub, where the file can be checked against its digest. The command below recomputes one headline value from a committed state file with the record's own estimator.

  • The data layer behind this page was checked by re-reading every quoted value at its cited line: 2571 assertions passed over 2223 source references.
  • The views behind the errata, the lessons and the withheld files were checked the same way: 377 of 377 references found at their cited line, with their file's digest.
  • The two record files quoted on the front page, the root README and the prior art map, are copies of the files at the tag kept beside the data; the README copy's digest must equal the files table's entry, and the map's digest is listed there.

The record's own worked example recomputes F-22 from a clone with numpy; its command, from the root README:

cd sideband
python - <<'EOF'
import json, sys, numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, 'src')
from sideband.stats import paired_ratio_delta_ci
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open('results/real/oq16_stage_r.json.state.jsonl') if l.strip()][1:]
A = lambda a: [r for r in rows if r['arm'] == a and r['variant'] == 'live']
f, t = A('free'), A('tel')
print(paired_ratio_delta_ci([r['sse'] for r in f], [r['count'] for r in f],
                            [r['sse'] for r in t], [r['count'] for r in t], n_boot=2000, seed=0))
print(json.load(open('results/real/oq16_stage_r.json'))['delta_free']['live'])
EOF
